Q1. Discuss the major goals of AI - perception, reasoning, planning, communication,
creativity, learning, and control/manipulation - and explain how Generative AI is
contributing to these goals.
Answer. Artificial Intelligence aims to build systems that can perceive the world, form useful
internal representations, reason about alternatives, act toward goals, communicate with humans,
learn from experience, and manipulate digital or physical environments. Generative AI contributes
strongly because it learns data distributions and can produce new content rather than only assign￾ing labels. 1. Perception: Perception is the ability to interpret inputs such as images, audio,
video, text, and sensor measurements. Generative models can learn rich representations of such
inputs and can reconstruct, synthesize, denoise, complete, or transform them. For example, a
diffusion model can learn the visual structure of images and then generate an image from a text
description. 2. Reasoning: Reasoning requires forming relationships among facts and drawing
conclusions. Large generative models can represent patterns from large corpora and generate in￾termediate explanations, hypotheses, or candidate solutions. In practical systems, generation is
often combined with retrieval, tools, search, or symbolic checks so that the generated reasoning is
grounded in external evidence. 3. Planning: Planning means selecting a sequence of actions that
moves a system from an initial state to a desired goal. Generative models can propose candidate
action sequences, simulate possible outcomes, or generate sub-goals. The generated plan can then
be verified by a planner, simulator, or constraint checker. 4. Communication: Generative models
naturally support language generation, translation, summarization, dialogue, question answering,
and multimodal interaction. This allows a machine to communicate information in a form suitable
for a human or another agent. 5. Creativity: Generative AI can synthesize novel text, images,
music, video, 3D assets, software code, and design candidates. The key point is that the output is
newly generated from learned statistical structure rather than simply retrieved as an exact stored
example. 6. Learning: Generative models learn a representation of the underlying data distri￾bution. Learning may be supervised, weakly supervised, or unsupervised. Latent-variable models
are especially useful because they can discover hidden factors of variation and provide compact
representations. 7. Control and manipulation: A generative model can serve as a simulator or
world model, predicting plausible future states and helping an agent choose actions. In robotics,
for example, a model can generate predicted observations under candidate actions. The actual
control loop still requires feedback and safety constraints. Overall, Generative AI expands AI from
classification and prediction toward synthesis and simulation. It is therefore useful as a component
of systems that perceive, reason, plan, communicate, create, learn, and act. Exam Tip: In an
exam, connect each AI goal to one clear generative capability and one concrete application. This
makes the answer both conceptual and application-oriented.
3

Q2. Explain the major capabilities of Generative AI with its major applications. Ex￾plain how the scaling of Generative AI models depends on data, model parameters,
computational resources, memory, and distributed training. Discuss why scaling be￾comes increasingly challenging as model size increases.
Answer. Generative AI learns a probability distribution over data and can then sample or condi￾tion the learned distribution to create new outputs. Its major capabilities include text generation,
image generation, audio/music synthesis, video generation, code generation, multimodal generation,
data augmentation, completion, inpainting, style transfer, and simulation. Text: writing, summa￾rization, translation, tutoring, question answering, code generation. Images: text-to-image, image
completion, editing, super-resolution, synthetic data generation. Audio and music: speech syn￾thesis, voice conversion, music generation, sound effects. Video: text-to-video, video continuation,
editing, avatar generation. Multimodal: generating or transforming combinations of text, images,
audio, and video. Scientific/engineering uses: molecular design, synthetic datasets, simulation,
inverse design, and reconstruction. Scaling depends on several interacting resources: Data scale:
Larger models generally need more diverse, high-quality data. Insufficient or repetitive data limits
generalization and can increase overfitting or memorization. Model parameters: Increasing pa￾rameters increases representational capacity. More parameters allow the model to represent more
complex functions, but also increase training and inference cost. Compute: Training requires
matrix operations over many examples and many optimization steps. Compute therefore grows
with model size, data size, sequence length, and number of training steps. Memory: Parameters,
optimizer states, activations, gradients, and temporary buffers must be stored. Optimizer state can
require several times the memory of the parameter tensors. Distributed training: Large models
are split across multiple accelerators using data parallelism, tensor/model parallelism, or pipeline
parallelism. Communication and synchronization become major system costs. Why scaling gets
harder: Memory pressure grows because parameters and training states may no longer fit on one
device. Communication overhead grows as devices exchange activations, gradients, or parameters.
Training becomes more sensitive to data quality, optimization stability, and numerical precision.
Inference also becomes expensive because every generated token or output sample may require
many large matrix operations. The practical bottleneck shifts from pure arithmetic to the com￾plete system: memory bandwidth, network bandwidth, synchronization, storage, and reliability.
Exam Tip: Remember the central idea: scaling is not only about buying a larger model. Data,
parameters, compute, memory, and communication must scale together.

Q4. Explain the major challenges in deep generative modeling, particularly for high￾dimensional data such as images. Explain how these challenges affect the ability to
generate realistic samples and perform discriminative tasks.
Answer. High-dimensional data create a very large sample space. A 64 x 64 RGB image already
has 64 x 64 x 3 pixel values; the number of possible images is enormous. Learning a useful dis￾tribution over that space is therefore much harder than learning a distribution over a small set
of scalar variables. Curse of dimensionality: Data become sparse in high-dimensional space,
so enormous amounts of training data may be needed. Complex dependencies: Pixels are not
independent; edges, shapes, textures, object parts, lighting, and semantics interact across many
spatial scales. Likelihood difficulty: Exact likelihoods may be hard or expensive to compute
for complex models. Optimization difficulty: Deep non-convex objectives can have unstable
gradients and sensitive hyperparameters. Mode coverage: A model may generate sharp samples
but miss important modes of the real distribution, or generate diverse outputs that lack realism.
Representation quality: A poor latent representation can hurt interpolation, controllability,
and downstream classification. These challenges affect generation because unrealistic or repeated
samples appear when the learned distribution is poor. They affect discrimination because a genera￾tive representation may fail to preserve class-relevant factors. Conversely, a well-learned generative
representation can provide useful features for classification, clustering, semi-supervised learning, or
retrieval.

Q1. Explain the motivation for using latent variable models. For the image example,
answer (a)-(d).
Answer. Latent variable models introduce hidden variables z that explain underlying structure in
observed data x. This is useful because high-dimensional observations often arise from a smaller
number of meaningful causes or factors. Instead of modeling every pixel directly, a model can first
represent latent factors such as identity, pose, lighting, gender, or hair color and then generate
the image from them. (a) Observed versus latent variables: x is the observed image and z
contains hidden variables or latent factors. The training data may contain x but not direct labels
for z. (b) High-level factors: z can encode semantically meaningful variations. For example,
one component or direction of z may correlate with pose, another with hair color, and another
with lighting. In an ideal disentangled representation, changing one factor would have a focused
semantic effect. (c) Generative model 𝑝(𝑥 ∣ 𝑧): Given a latent state z, the decoder models how
an image could be generated. This conditional problem can be simpler because z summarizes the
important causes. The full data distribution is obtained by integrating/summing over z:
𝑝(𝑥) = ∫ 𝑝(𝑥 ∣ 𝑧)𝑝(𝑧) 𝑑𝑧
(d) Posterior 𝑝(𝑧 ∣ 𝑥): The posterior tells us which latent configurations explain an observed
image. Learning or approximating this posterior provides an unsupervised representation of the
data. The latent vector can then be used for clustering, visualization, interpolation, reconstruction,
or downstream tasks.

Q5. Discuss major practical GAN training challenges, including unstable optimization
and mode collapse. Explain oscillating losses and empirical mitigation approaches.
Answer. GAN training is a two-player game rather than an ordinary single-objective optimization
problem. The generator and discriminator continually adapt to one another, so the target seen by
one network changes as the other is updated. Unstable optimization: If D becomes too strong, G
may receive weak or unhelpful gradients in some formulations. If G improves too quickly, D can be￾come inaccurate. The balance can therefore oscillate rather than converge smoothly. Oscillating
losses: GAN losses need not decrease monotonically. A decrease in discriminator loss can make
generator loss increase and vice versa. Moreover, the numerical value of a GAN loss depends on
the current opponent, so it is not a standalone quality score. Mode collapse: The generator maps
many different latent vectors to similar outputs. The samples may look realistic but fail to cover
the diversity of the real data distribution. Example: a face generator repeatedly produces faces
with very similar pose, hairstyle, and background while ignoring other valid variations. Empiri￾cal mitigation: commonly used approaches include improved discriminator regularization, careful
learning-rate/𝛽 tuning, minibatch-based diversity mechanisms, feature matching, alternative adver￾sarial objectives, spectral normalization, gradient penalties, data augmentation, and architectural
changes. No single method guarantees complete elimination of collapse.

Q7. Explain why evaluating generative models is challenging and how evaluation de￾pends on the intended task. Cover density estimation, sampling, latent representation
learning, and downstream applications.
Answer. No single evaluation score captures all aspects of a generative model. A model may
have good likelihood but produce visually weak samples, or produce visually impressive samples
while missing modes of the true distribution. Evaluation must therefore match the intended use.
Density estimation: Evaluate likelihood or held-out log-likelihood when the model explicitly
provides a tractable or comparable density. The goal is whether the learned probability model
assigns appropriate probability to unseen data. Sampling/generation: Evaluate realism, diver￾sity, fidelity, coverage, and human or task-specific quality. Image metrics such as IS and FID are
common, but they are imperfect proxies. Latent representation learning: Evaluate whether la￾tent codes capture meaningful factors, support smooth interpolation, clustering, reconstruction, or
disentanglement. Downstream applications: Evaluate the actual task, such as semi-supervised
classification, image translation, retrieval, completion, augmentation, or domain adaptation. The
generated data or latent representation should improve the target application rather than only
score well on a generic metric.

Q1. Explain the architecture and working principle of a Conditional GAN (cGAN).
How does conditioning on class information modify a conventional GAN? Explain
text-to-image use.
Answer. A conditional GAN adds an observed condition y, such as a class label or text description,
to both the generator and discriminator. Instead of learning G(z), the generator learns G(z,y), while
the discriminator evaluates whether a sample is real and whether it is consistent with y.

For class-conditional image generation, y could be the label “cat” or “car”. The generator receives z
and y and creates an image matching the requested class. For text-to-image synthesis, y is replaced
by a learned text embedding; the generator uses that embedding as semantic conditioning and D
checks image-text compatibility as part of its discrimination task.

Q2. Explain the motivation behind BiGAN. Describe how G and E learn the joint
distributions of (X,Z), and state the inverse-mapping condition.
Answer. A conventional GAN learns to map z to x but does not naturally provide the inverse
mapping from an observed x back to a latent z. A Bidirectional GAN (BiGAN) introduces an
encoder E(x) to infer a latent representation from real data. The discriminator receives pairs
rather than single samples. From the generator path it sees (z,G(z)). From the encoder path it
sees (E(x),x). The discriminator learns to distinguish these two joint distributions, while G and
E learn together to make them indistinguishable. joint_1: (z, G(z)), joint_2: (E(x), x) When
training is successful and the mappings are compatible, E and G become approximately inverse on
the data manifold: 𝐸(𝐺(𝑧)) ≈ 𝑧 and 𝐺(𝐸(𝑥)) ≈ 𝑥 for relevant samples. BiGAN therefore supports
both sample generation and latent inference.

Q3. CoGAN for two semantically related but unpaired domains X_A and X_B: ex￾plain learning without correspondence supervision, weight sharing, and one limitation.
Answer. CoGAN uses two GAN-style networks, one per domain, and couples them through
shared parameters. The domains may contain related semantic objects but there are no paired
examples saying which image in A corresponds to which image in B. The domain-specific parts
capture low-level appearance differences, while shared layers encourage the two networks to encode
common high-level semantics. Because shared parameters are trained from both domains, the model
can learn a common latent structure without explicit image-to-image correspondences. Weight
sharing is an inductive bias: if high-level concepts such as “object category” are common across
domains, sharing deeper layers encourages the networks to discover representations useful to both.
Earlier layers are often left separate because low-level statistics such as color, texture, and contrast
may differ by domain. Limitation: CoGAN relies on the assumption that the two domains share
useful high-level semantics. If their underlying structures differ strongly, the shared representation
may be inappropriate; training can also be sensitive to the domain gap and adversarial optimization.

Q6. Explain BiGAN motivation, compare with conventional GAN, roles of G/E/D,
joint discrimination, and how a trained BiGAN supports generation and inference.
Answer. The key addition in BiGAN is an encoder E that maps observed data to latent space. A
conventional GAN has G:z->x but no explicit learned inverse x->z. BiGAN learns both directions
through a joint adversarial game. G: generates x from z. E: maps x to a latent representation

whether z or x is individually real. Instead, it checks whether the pair has been produced by
the generator side or the encoder/data side. When the joint distributions match, the encoder
and generator are approximately inverse on the relevant manifolds. After training, generation is
performed by sampling z and computing G(z). Representation inference is performed by taking a
real x and computing E(x). This makes BiGAN useful when both synthesis and latent embeddings
are required.
